newsitem.title: ZAIRE: FEATURE - Soldiers of fortune -- Zaire's open secret.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Soldiers of fortune -- Zaire's open secret.

text.p: The shrouded body of a white mercenary killed fighting rebels in eastern Zaire arrived by helicopter into the jungle city of Kisangani over the weekend, witnesses say.
The body had been hidden at a textile factory prior to being sent back to Europe, they add.
The sighting offered further evidence that Zaire was employing up to 300 soldiers of fortune, many of them Serbs from former Yugoslavia, to help recapture territory held by rebels.
There's no denying the presence of armed white men in combat fatigues in the headquarter city for Zaire's counter-offensive.
"They are not mercenaries. They are sent by foreign allies as assistants and instructors for the army," an army colonel in Kisangani maintained.
But security sources and informed inhabitants say the bulk of the whites who have arrived since December have already been sent to fighting positions closer to rebel-held territory.
A senior dignitary from the Upper Zaire region told Reuters that their initial goal would be to back the army in a bid to recapture the main airstrips in rebel hands.
At the $120 dollar a night Palm Beach hotel on the banks of the vast river Zaire, mercenaries, led by a Belgian one-time associate of French soldier of fortune Bob Denard, can be seen playing cards.
Elsewhere in Kisangani, helicopters buzz over crumbling termite-eaten buildings on their way out on frequent raids.
Sources close to the army chief of staff, General Mahele Lieko Bokungo, said eastern European pilots fly newly acquired MI24 Russian combat helicopters.

Veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko, in power since a 1965 coup, appointed Mahele in December on returning from Europe after cancer surgery in August. He revamped both the army command and the government to take the fight to the rebels.
The Tutsi-led rebels, who launched their revolt in October accusing Zaire of denying them citizenship, hold towns and territory along the border with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda.
The government said last week its troops had retaken the town of Walekale 120 km (80 miles) from rebel leader Laurent Kabila's Goma headquarters after killing 100 rebels.
The sources close to Mahele said the MI24s strafed a column of rebels in the battle for the town. The sources said rebels had attempted to advance up the one passable road to Kisangani.
Rebel positions over 100 km (70 miles) from the strategic mining centre of Bunia, were bombarded from the sky over the weekend, Kisangani inhabitants in radio contact with Bunia say.
There were also reports of fighting from around Wamba 400 km (250 miles) north east of Kisangani.
Artillery cannons and three small fighter jets on the airport tarmac at Kisangani give a further clue as to Zaire's reserve firepower.

Hundreds of ageing Katangese gendarmes, veterans of secessionist rebellions in the copper-rich province of Shaba in the 1960s and 1970s, have been re-armed to fight alongside the regular army they once fought against.

"We are here as nationalists, fighting in this war to push back foreign rebels who have stepped into our country," said a smiling but toothless gendarme of 65. He was wounded when rebels took Bunia at the beginning of January.

Kisangani airport is a constant hive of activity. Hundreds of regular soldiers with heavy back packs, each with two grenades pinned on either side of their new combat jackets, filed onto planes on Saturday.

But older inhabitants of the crumbling riverside town whose devastated economy has been further depressed by the latest crisis sit with bottles of locally brewed Primus beer resigned to what seems to many of them to be history repeating itself.

"We have seen mercenaries here before. In the 1960s there was (Jean) Schramme (a Belgian who helped to suppress a 1964 rebellion). There was Bob Denard. But the rebellions they suppressed were at the beginning of Mobutu's reign," one ageing Kisangani trader mused.
"Now that it is coming to an end we don't know what awaits us next."
